newsitem.title: USA: US stocks seen steady but Dow open a question mark.
newsitem.headline: US stocks seen steady but Dow open a question mark.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open generally steady, but some follow-through could be in store for blue chips after Tuesday's last-minute sell-off.

While analysts said selling pressure could continue to afflict the Dow industrials, which have tallied scorching gains over the last few months, worries about a major Dow correction remain at bay for now.
"There could be some more selling in blue chips but this shake-up has not reverberated around the globe," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities.
"I think people realize that 80 points in the Dow at these levels is not such a big deal," Wachtel said.

Analysts found reason to be optimistic because the largely program-driven sell-off, which knocked 79 points off the Dow, did not spill over to the entire market. The Nasdaq Composite, for example, finished slightly higher on the session.
"I welcomed yesterday's decline," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "A good sign was that the broader market held up while blue chips felt the pinch."

Cardillo also noted reports of merger talks between Delta Air Lines Inc and Continental Airlines Inc could prompt buying in transportation stocks today, another group that bucked the trend by finishing higher on Tuesday.

As for blue chips themselves, analysts seemed content to await the outcome of today's session. While none would predict outright a Dow decline for the session, they generally agreed another couple of percent would hardly be cause for alarm.
"If it does fall back from 6500 to 6200, is it a calamity?" said Wachtel. "I say no, I say it's a good thing."
In Tokyo, stocks ended little changed after a directionless session. The benchmark Nikkei-225 index rose 29 points to 20,660.
In London, the FTSE 100 fell 22 points to 4040. U.S. stocks were generally firmer but volume was thin.
The dollar was trading at just above its lows in Tokyo, where it dipped to about 113.4 yen. The greenback held near session highs in Europe, hovering just over 1.56 marks.
U.S. Treasuries were barely changed. The 30-year bond was unchanged, yielding 6.37 percent.
The December S&P 500 index future rose 0.90 to 746.40.

The New York Times Marketplace column examines the prospects of Tele-Communications Inc's latest spin-off. The paper reports the new company, TCI Satellite Entertainment, faces a stiff competitive environment.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column writes that as the tax-loss selling season reaches its peak, investors are likely to begin sifting through the losers' list for opportunities.
